## Recent Releases and Industry Adoption

OpenAI released Structured Outputs in August 2024 with response_format: { type: "json_schema" }, Google Gemini added response_schema at Google I/O in May 2024, and Anthropic followed in November 2025 with constrained decoding for Claude.

## Key Technical Developments

Constrained decoding enforces validity during generation by masking invalid tokens at every step, including lexically CD, finite-state CD, and systems that integrate grammar engines such as XGrammar and Outlines.

Recent approaches address calibration issues: Grammar-Aligned Decoding (2024) tackles the issue of filtering tokens distorting the model's probability distribution, with their method (ASAp) reweighting sampling so the model behaves as if trained with the grammar.

## Performance Improvements

IterGen (ICLR 2025) introduces forward/backward generation tied to grammar symbols with KV-cache reuse for efficient "undo and redo", enabling faster corrections for interactive use like code co-pilots.

XGrammar is the default structured generation backend for vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM as of March 2026, achieving under 40 microseconds per token with near-zero overhead in JSON generation.

## Benchmarking Work

Recent constrained-decoding frameworks such as Guidance, Outlines, and XGrammar provide broad support for different types of constraints, minimal overhead, and compatibility with various LM ecosystems, with comprehensive benchmarks being published in late 2024 and early 2025.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about "Grammar-Aligned Decoding":

## Overview

Grammar-Aligned Decoding (GAD) addresses a key problem: while constrained decoding approaches restrict LLM outputs to match a given grammar, these techniques can distort the LLM's distribution, leading to grammatical outputs with likelihoods that are not proportional to the original LLM's distribution.

## The ASAp Algorithm

The paper proposes adaptive sampling with approximate expected futures (ASAp), a decoding algorithm that guarantees the output to be grammatical while provably producing outputs that match the conditional probability of the LLM's distribution conditioned on the given grammar constraint. The algorithm uses prior sample outputs to soundly overapproximate the future grammaticality of different output prefixes.

## Publication Details

The work was published on September 25, 2024 as a NeurIPS 2024 poster presentation.

## Evaluation

The authors evaluated ASAp on two structured prediction tasks: formal program synthesis and constituency parsing, demonstrating that their approach better respects the LLM while still enforcing grammar constraints compared to traditional GCD techniques.

You can find the full paper on ArXiv (arxiv.org/abs/2405.21047) or the NeurIPS proceedings page for the complete BibTeX citation and additional details.

Based on the search results, I found the paper you're looking for. The document is titled "Exploiting Class Similarity for Machine Learning with Confidence Labels and Projective Loss Functions" by Gautam Rajendrakumar Gare and John Michael Galeotti from Carnegie Mellon University, published in 2021.

The key contribution of this paper is the introduction of confidence labels, which are probabilistic labels denoting the likelihood of similarity, or confusability, between classes. Class similarity among classes is often the cause of poor model performance due to models confusing between them, and current labeling techniques fail to explicitly capture such similarity information.

The paper proposes projective loss functions designed to work with confidence labels with an ability to relax the loss penalty for errors that confuse similar classes. The authors use this approach to train neural networks with noisy labels, based on the belief that noisy labels are partly a result of confusability arising from class similarity.

The paper is available on arXiv (2103.13607) and was published in March 2021.
